    The 14 GPCM Covariance Models¶

    This notebook demonstrates the Phase 3 (v0.4 roadmap) addition: all 14 Celeux & Govaert (1995) Gaussian Parsimonious Clustering Models (GPCM) -- the same family mclust implements -- as covariance_type options on GaussianMixture, plus select_model's mclust-style default of sweeping all 14 codes.

    See the GPCM Covariance Models user guide for what each of the 14 codes means.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import numpy as np
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import os

os.chdir('../')

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from tgmm import GaussianMixture, select_model
from tgmm.covariance.gpcm import GPCM_CODES
from tgmm.plotting import plot_gmm

random_state = 42
    import numpy as np import torch import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import os os.chdir('../') from sklearn.datasets import load_iris from tgmm import GaussianMixture, select_model from tgmm.covariance.gpcm import GPCM_CODES from tgmm.plotting import plot_gmm random_state = 42

    Part 1: the classic iris petal measurements (2-D)¶

    Petal length and width, the two features that most cleanly separate the 3 iris species -- small enough to sweep all 14 models x several K quickly, and 2-D enough to plot the winning model's component ellipses directly.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    iris = load_iris()
X_iris = torch.tensor(iris.data[:, [2, 3]], dtype=torch.float64)  # petal length, petal width

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
plt.scatter(X_iris[:, 0], X_iris[:, 1], c=iris.target, cmap='viridis', s=15)
plt.xlabel('petal length (cm)')
plt.ylabel('petal width (cm)')
plt.title('Iris petal measurements (true species)')
plt.show()

    BIC by model family and K¶

    One line per covariance code, BIC against K -- lower is better.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
for code_name in GPCM_CODES:
    sub = df_iris[df_iris['covariance_type'] == code_name].sort_values('n_components')
    sub = sub.dropna(subset=['bic'])
    if len(sub) == 0:
        continue
    plt.plot(sub['n_components'], sub['bic'], marker='o', markersize=3, label=code_name, alpha=0.7)
plt.xlabel('n_components (K)')
plt.ylabel('BIC (lower is better)')
plt.title('BIC across all 14 GPCM models, iris petal data')
plt.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=8)
plt.show()

best = result_iris.best_
print(f'Winning model: {best.covariance_type_} (K={best.n_components}), BIC={best.bic(X_iris):.2f}')

    Part 2: a 10-D latent-space-like dataset¶

    Four clusters in 10 dimensions with deliberately varied covariance structure (different volumes, some axis-aligned, some correlated/elongated) -- the kind of thing a GPCM sweep is actually for: no single covariance type is obviously right, so the model-selection search has real work to do.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    def make_latent_cluster(n, d, seed, volume, elongation=None, rotate=False):
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    base = torch.randn(n, d, generator=gen, dtype=torch.float64)
    scale = torch.ones(d, dtype=torch.float64)
    if elongation is not None:
        scale[: len(elongation)] = torch.tensor(elongation, dtype=torch.float64)
    X = base * scale.sqrt() * volume
    if rotate:
        Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(torch.randn(d, d, generator=gen, dtype=torch.float64))
        X = X @ Q.T
    return X

torch.manual_seed(random_state)
d = 10
centers = torch.randn(4, d, dtype=torch.float64) * 6
clusters = [
    make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=1, volume=1.0) + centers[0],
    make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=2, volume=1.8) + centers[1],
    make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=3, volume=1.0, elongation=[4, 4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) + centers[2],
    make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=4, volume=1.0, elongation=[4, 4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1], rotate=True) + centers[3],
]
X_latent = torch.cat(clusters, dim=0)
print(X_latent.shape)
    def make_latent_cluster(n, d, seed, volume, elongation=None, rotate=False): gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed) base = torch.randn(n, d, generator=gen, dtype=torch.float64) scale = torch.ones(d, dtype=torch.float64) if elongation is not None: scale[: len(elongation)] = torch.tensor(elongation, dtype=torch.float64) X = base * scale.sqrt() * volume if rotate: Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(torch.randn(d, d, generator=gen, dtype=torch.float64)) X = X @ Q.T return X torch.manual_seed(random_state) d = 10 centers = torch.randn(4, d, dtype=torch.float64) * 6 clusters = [ make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=1, volume=1.0) + centers[0], make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=2, volume=1.8) + centers[1], make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=3, volume=1.0, elongation=[4, 4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) + centers[2], make_latent_cluster(150, d, seed=4, volume=1.0, elongation=[4, 4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1], rotate=True) + centers[3], ] X_latent = torch.cat(clusters, dim=0) print(X_latent.shape)

    BIC vs ICL for the winning K¶

    Both criteria, compared across models at the BIC-winning K.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    best_latent = result_latent.best_
winning_k = best_latent.n_components
print(f'Winning model: {best_latent.covariance_type_} (K={winning_k}), '
      f'BIC={best_latent.bic(X_latent):.2f}, ICL={best_latent.icl(X_latent):.2f}')

at_k = df_latent[df_latent['n_components'] == winning_k].dropna(subset=['bic', 'icl']).sort_values('bic')
at_k[['covariance_type', 'bic', 'icl', 'converged']].head(8)

    Takeaways¶

    • select_model's default sweep (all 14 GPCM codes) finds a sensible winner without having to guess a covariance structure up front -- VVE-ish results on the iris data (shared orientation, elongated per-species shapes) are a well-known finding for this dataset.
    • On genuinely mixed-structure data (axis-aligned vs. correlated clusters, Part 2), no single covariance type dominates at every K -- exactly the situation the 14-model family is for.
    • volume_/shape_/orientation_ on the winning model expose why it won, not just that it did -- see the user guide for how to read them.
